newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian police prevent anti-government rallies.
newsitem.headline: Albanian police prevent anti-government rallies.

text.p: Police were out in force on Sunday to watch over rallies by a handful of Albanians demanding the dismissal of the right-wing government and compensation for savings lost in failed pyramid investment schemes.

But residents of Europe's poorest country were clearly cowed by a crackdown after violent protests last week in which enraged investors set fire to government buildings. Many ruined would-be demonstrators chose this time to stay home.

In Tirana, scores of uniformed and plainclothes police cordoned off roads leading to a soccer pitch where a trade union rally had been due to take place. The main organiser, one of the heroes of the successful bid to topple hardline communists in 1990, was manhandled and taken away by police.
About 500 people turned out for a demonstration in a stadium in the Adriatic port of Durres. Police swarmed around the area on foot and in vans but kept their distance.
A third rally was scheduled in Lezhe, further north, but there were no reports on how it proceeded.

In Tirana, a few hundred yards from the playing field where the protest was to be staged, police remonstrated with trade union leader Azem Hajdari before bundling him into a car. He was released soon after.
"They're not letting me go any further," Hajdari said in an interview. Police said organisers had failed to secure necessary permission.
Hajdari accuses the government of mishandling the pyramid schemes in which virtually every Albanian family had a stake.

But he remains close to President Sali Berisha. The president has promised that the poorest investors in two of the dubious schemes will start getting compensation this week, some in cash, others in government certificates.

A member of parliament who enjoys immunity from prosecution, Hajdari said police had arrested his brother as well as the secretary general of his trade union confederation. He said his family had received telephone threats.
He was among student leaders who led 1990 protests against the communists who inherited power from hardliner Enver Hoxha, who ruled for 40 years and kept Albania in total isolation.

Albanians are clearly wary after the arrest of at least 149 people on public order charges following last weekend's mass protests. Prosecutors say those convicted could face at least 15 years in prison.
One senior opposition Socialist was mysteriously beaten up in central Tirana on Wednesday by unknown assailants.
Thousands demonstrated in central Tirana last Sunday, hurling stones and clashing with riot police who broke up the protest by force.
One elderly man in Durres said there were three reasons why so few people had attended the latest rally.

"Firstly, there were so many police outside the stadium, secondly because the Democrats here have warned people that if they demonstrate they will lose their state jobs, and thirdly, because of the arrests."

Small cracks have begun appearing in the dominant Democratic Party, but it remains in firm control of parliament after winning a general election last year criticised by Western organisers as rife with irregularities.
